scenario.prompt_to_agent:
PC11-14 in Location C (192.168.200.x) report they cannot reach
Location A (172.16.10.x, 172.16.20.x) at all. Other zones can
still reach each other. Find what isolated Location C.

injection.action: shut down BOTH of router4's upstream links -- Location C is dual-homed (eth5 -> router3 over 172.25.1.x AND eth4 -> router5 over 192.168.15.x); both must drop to isolate it
injection.command:
ip link set eth5 down
  ip link set eth4 down

pre_check.command: ip -br link show eth5 | grep -c UP

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth5 | grep -c UP
ip -br link show eth4 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router4 uplinks eth5 (-> router3,
  172.25.1.0/24) AND eth4 (-> router5, 192.168.15.0/24)
Mechanism: router4 (Location C's edge) is DUAL-HOMED to the rest
  of the network -- via router3 over 172.25.1.0/24 (eth5) AND via
  router5 over 192.168.15.0/24 (eth4). Cutting only one uplink
  reroutes over the other with no outage, so BOTH must be down to
  isolate Location C. With both down, RIP withdraws every path and
  Location C loses Locations A and B.
Localization: router4 (both uplinks, eth5 and eth4)
Root cause: both of router4's upstream links are down
  (eth5 -> router3 and eth4 -> router5)
Fix: `ip link set eth5 up; ip link set eth4 up` on router4
scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set eth5 up; ip link set eth4 up` on router4
scoring_axes: must-identify-affected-link: router4's two uplinks (eth5 -> router3 and eth4 -> router5)

line.command: ip -br link show eth5 | grep -c UP
ip -br link show eth4 | grep -c UP

agent.diagnosis_text:
Router4 is the sole gateway for Location C (192.168.200.0/24). Its two
uplink interfaces — eth4 (192.168.15.2/24, segment link_r4_r5 toward
router5) and eth5 (172.25.1.1/24, segment link_r4_r3 toward router3) —
were administratively brought down after the lab started. The startup
script correctly issues `ip link set eth4 up` and `ip link set eth5 up`,
so both interfaces came up at boot and RIP converged normally. A
post-startup injection then executed `ip link set eth4 down` and
`ip link set eth5 down` on router4, collapsing both uplinks simultaneously.
With no active physical-layer path to either router3 or router5, RIP
loses all its neighbours on router4: the FRR RIP table shrinks to a
single entry (`C(i) 192.168.200.0/24 self`) and the kernel routing table
contains nothing beyond the directly-connected LAN. The static default
route (`via 172.25.1.2`) configured in startup is also silently withdrawn
by the kernel when eth5 goes down, leaving router4 with literally zero
forwarding knowledge outside its own segment. Router3's RIP table
confirms the isolation: its 192.168.200.0/24 entry (learned from
172.25.1.1) is expiring (timer 00:29), while Location A prefixes
(172.16.10.0/24, 172.16.20.0/24) remain fresh via router2, proving the
rest of the network is healthy. The corrective fix is to restore both
interfaces on router4: `ip link set eth4 up && ip link set eth5 up`. RIP
will re-establish adjacencies with router3 and router5 within one update
cycle (~30 s) and full reachability to Location A will be restored.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-affected-link: router4's two uplinks (eth5 -> router3 and eth4 -> router5)
per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly names both affected interfaces—eth5 (to router3) and eth4 (to router5)—and explains they were brought down, matching the expected affected links.
The agent recommends bringing eth4 and eth5 back up on router4 (ip link set eth4 up && ip link set eth5 up), which matches the expected fix to restore connectivity.

The investigation log contains direct observations (ip link, FRR interface and routing outputs, startup file contents, and neighboring routers' state) that support the diagnosis that both of router4's uplinks are down and that this caused Location C's isolation; a minor unobserved inference (exact mechanism of who/what ran the down commands) is phrased as likely rather than proven.
